findings.issue_text: [BUG] The new gate `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` references `organization_context`, a name that does not exist anywhere in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get` (the method has no such parameter, no local assignment, and no import defines it), so evaluating the expression raises NameError for every non-superuser. Every GET /api/0/organizations/<slug>/audit-logs/ from a non-superuser (i.e. all org members and admins using audit logs) 500s before pagination even runs — the `or` short-circuits only for superusers — which takes the endpoint down for its entire normal audience and makes the optimized-pagination branch unreachable by the very admins it targets.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil directly to the raw ordered attribute — with `order_by="-datetime"` from the audit-logs endpoint, self.key is "datetime" and getattr(item, "datetime") returns a datetime instance, which supports neither floor nor ceil, raising TypeError (DateTimePaginator's original get_item_key converts via strftime first; this copy dropped that step). build_cursor invokes key() on the first/last element of every non-empty result page, so any authorized admin requesting the endpoint with optimized_pagination=true against an organization that has at least one audit entry gets an unhandled TypeError and a 500 — the new paginator only completes successfully for organizations with zero audit rows.

[BUG] The `if self.enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0:` branch executes `list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with a negative start against a Django QuerySet, and QuerySet.__getitem__ raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` for slices with negative bounds — the in-code claim that "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false. Any request whose cursor carries a negative offset (sentry cursors are unsigned value:offset:is_prev strings a client can craft freely) dies with an AssertionError and a 500, so the advertised negative-offset capability can never succeed against the ORM-backed queryset this endpoint passes in — the feature branch is unexecutable as written.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result duplicates BasePaginator.get_result wholesale (~65 lines including the prev-cursor dedup and offset arithmetic) instead of overriding only the slicing, and the two copies already disagree: the base-class rewrite at paginator.py:179-184 clamps negative forward offsets to 0 while this copy's advanced branch deliberately permits them. The next fix to paginator edge-case handling (prev-cursor filtering and offset math, code with a history of subtle bugs in this file) will land in one copy and silently miss the other; the shared-base edit also changes slicing semantics for every paginator in Sentry (OffsetPaginator, DateTimePaginator, SequencePaginator and all subclass users): a negative forward-offset cursor that previously raised Django's negative-slice AssertionError now silently returns page 1 instead of erroring.

[ADVISORY] The diff ships a brand-new endpoint request path (the optimized_pagination branch) and a brand-new paginator class with zero tests — no test file is touched anywhere in the diff. The untested path is exactly where the blocking crashes live (the organization_context NameError on line 71 and the get_item_key TypeError), and a single API test exercising optimized_pagination=true would have surfaced both before merge; instead the endpoint's regression suite gains coverage only of the untouched legacy branch.

[ADVISORY] The new pagination behavior is gated solely on the raw query string `optimized_pagination=true` with no feature flag or options entry, and the admin-permission expression on line 71 is evaluated unconditionally on every request even when the parameter is absent. Operators responding to an incident on the optimized path must deploy code rather than flip a flag, and every ordinary audit-log request pays an extra permission-chain evaluation (today, the NameError) on a control-silo endpoint for a feature the request never opted into.

[ADVISORY] The cursors.py hunk adds only two comments ("Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets…") while `self.offset = int(offset)` is byte-for-byte unchanged, so the file implements nothing — Cursor already accepted negative integers before this PR. The change record asserts cursor semantics were altered in utils/cursors.py as a prerequisite of the feature, so an auditor or follow-up maintainer tracing the negative-offset support lands on a no-op hunk and must rediscover that the only real gating lives in the paginator slicing code, which clamps those very offsets.

[BUG] The new gate computes `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` against the bare name `organization_context`, which is never assigned in this method and never imported by this diff, so evaluating `enable_advanced` raises NameError whenever `request.user.is_superuser` is False. Every non-superuser request to GET /api/0/organizations/<slug>/audit-logs/ — i.e., the org owners and managers who are this endpoint's entire user base — returns a 500 instead of audit log data, because the gate is evaluated unconditionally before the `optimized_pagination` param is even consulted; the established sibling access flag already computed on this path by OrganizationAuditPermission (`request.access.has_global_access`) is what the author meant to read, and `.member` would additionally be None for users without membership.

[BUG] `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` applies `int(math.floor(value) if self._is_asc(for_prev) else math.ceil(value))` directly to the raw field value, and the only call site in this diff instantiates the class with `order_by="-datetime"` (organization_auditlogs.py line 80), so `value = getattr(item, "datetime")` is a `datetime` object and the floor/ceil arithmetic raises TypeError. Any authorized admin calling the audit-log endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` against an organization that has at least one AuditLogEntry gets a 500 — build_cursor invokes `key(results[0])` on every non-empty page — because the datetime-to-epoch conversion that DateTimePaginator (the paginator being replaced) exists to provide was never ported; the optimized path is dead on arrival.

[ADVISORY] The diff adds a request-time authorization gate, a new query parameter, and two paginator branches to the audit-log endpoint with no test anywhere in the diff — no test-shaped file appears in the diff at all — covering `optimized_pagination`, the `enable_advanced` computation, or either paginate branch. A single endpoint test exercising the new branch as an org admin would have caught both ship-blocking crashes this diff introduces (the `organization_context` NameError at line 71 and the datetime TypeError in get_item_key); with nothing added, the NameError that breaks the endpoint for every non-superuser ships completely undetected.

[BUG] `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value (`return cursor.value`, a string parsed from the `?cursor=` query param) instead of the `int(...)` cast the parent CursorPaginator performs, so string values like "1712345678" flow into `build_queryset`'s `datetime__lt/__gt` filters. Every cursor-bearing (page-2 and later) request on the optimized path fails when the queryset is evaluated at `list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`: Django's DateTimeField raises ValidationError ('value has an invalid format') for the non-ISO numeric string, producing a 500 — pagination beyond the first page is impossible on the optimized path even after the get_item_key crash is fixed.

[BUG] The negative-offset branch evaluates `list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset = cursor.offset < 0`, and slicing an unevaluated Django QuerySet with a negative bound raises AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported'). The one 'advanced feature' the class advertises throws a 500 for every negative offset it claims to support — a superuser client sending `?cursor=<value>:-5:1&optimized_pagination=true` hits the assert — and the inline comment asserting 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' (line 876) is false, so the mechanism can never work as designed.

[ADVISORY] `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a ~90-line new paginator class introduced with zero unit tests — no cursor round-trip test through `value_from_cursor`, no negative-offset slicing test, and no parity test asserting it returns the same rows and cursors as the DateTimePaginator it replaces. The negative-slicing AssertionError (lines 877-882), the string-cursor ValidationError (lines 842-843), and the get_item_key TypeError (lines 838-840) all ship undetected; a future maintainer modifying the copied offset/dedup math has no regression baseline, and a regression breaks the audit-log API for exactly the admins the feature targets.

[ADVISORY] The PR's stated requirement — enhanced pagination performance for high-volume audit logs — has no acceptance criterion anywhere in the diff: no benchmark, load test, or query measurement, and `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` executes the identical query pattern (build_queryset filter plus `queryset[start_offset:stop]` slice plus count_hits) as the paginator it replaces. The performance claim cannot be verified or falsified by reviewers or operators, so the only observable behavior changes this diff delivers are the crash paths above — the organization ships outage risk with zero delivered speedup, and any future 'is it actually faster?' investigation starts from no baseline.

[ADVISORY] The rewritten shared `get_result` lines claim 'This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' while deliberately passing negative client-supplied prev-cursor offsets (`offset` is left unclamped when `cursor.is_prev`) into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, which Django rejects with AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported'). The next developer extending bidirectional pagination on the strength of this comment builds on a mechanism that throws for every negative offset; and because these lines live in the shared offset paginator used by every offset-paginated endpoint in Sentry, the new `max(0, offset)` clamp also silently converts forged non-prev cursors from a 500 into a first-page response, leaving prev and non-prev cursor error behavior inconsistent with no documented rationale.

[ADVISORY] The new behavior is gated on a raw query parameter (`request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"`) with no feature flag, options entry, or API-schema declaration anywhere in the diff. When the optimized path throws (the datetime TypeError, the cursor ValidationError), there is no operator-level kill switch — restoring sane behavior for superuser API clients requires a code deploy — and clients sending `optimized_pagination=True` or `=1` silently get the old behavior, with no documented contract telling them the parameter exists or which values it accepts.

[BUG] This hunk silently changes slicing semantics of a pre-existing shared get_result (`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`) for every consumer of that paginator, not just the audit-log path this PR claims to optimize, and with a policy that contradicts the flag-gated handling the new class installs for the same case. A forward cursor carrying a negative offset - previously rejected by Django's `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` (500) at `queryset[offset:stop]` - now silently clamps to 0 and returns the dataset's first page, while the identical negative offset with is_prev still crashes; invalid client-crafted cursors (cursors are client-controlled base64) are half-accepted across all endpoints sharing this get_result, with no requirement in the PR tracing to this change.

[BUG] The `enable_advanced_features` negative-offset branch executes `list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with a negative start_offset, which Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ rejects with `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`, despite the in-code comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. A superuser/global-access caller hitting the audit-logs endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` and a cursor whose offset field is negative gets a 500; because no paginator code ever emits a negative offset, this crash is the branch's only reachable behavior, making the entire admin-gated 'advanced' feature ships-inert machinery whose one observable effect is an error response the code's own comment denies is possible.

[ADVISORY] The 'optimized' branch executes queries byte-identical to the default branch - OptimizedCursorPaginator's else path (paginator.py:884-886) is the same slicing, count, and build_cursor code as the DateTimePaginator it replaces - so the diff contains zero implementation of its stated requirement, 'Enhanced Pagination Performance for High-Volume Audit Logs'. Orgs with high-volume audit logs ship and operate a change they believe speeds up pagination while the SQL, hit counting, and serialization are unchanged; deleting the branch, the `optimized_pagination` param, the `enable_advanced_features` flag, and the entire ~95-line paginator class restores identical behavior for every cursor the API itself can produce, so the next engineer debugging a genuinely slow audit-log endpoint must first reverse-engineer that this knob is inert.

[ADVISORY] The diff introduces an undocumented public query parameter `optimized_pagination` plus an inline authorization gate (`request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`) into a documented public API endpoint, neither traceable to the PR's stated performance intent. Identical requests now take different paginator code paths depending on the caller's role - an API-contract inconsistency invisible in the docs/OpenAPI surface - and the forked permission check must now be maintained alongside the endpoint's existing OrganizationAuditPermission layer; `enable_advanced` is also evaluated unconditionally on every GET even when the parameter is absent, and with no options entry or feature flag the new behavior cannot be disabled without a code deploy.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator is a ~95-line copy of DateTimePaginator (get_item_key, value_from_cursor, and get_result are verbatim duplicates) whose shared slicing logic already diverged within this same PR (unconditional clamp at lines 179-184 vs. flag-gated at lines 877-886), and whose `enable_advanced_features` kwarg has exactly one call site passing the constant True. The next change to cursor semantics must be hand-applied to two copies of core pagination logic and the drift is already observable in this diff; inheriting from DateTimePaginator - or deleting the class outright, since the flag's default False value is never exercised by any caller - removes ~90 lines with zero reachable behavior change.

[ADVISORY] This hunk adds comments to the shared Cursor class asserting 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios' while leaving `self.offset = int(offset)` unchanged - a comment-only change publishing a contract that nothing in the PR enforces. Maintainers of the many paginators consuming Cursor read cursors.py:26-27 as sanctioning negative offsets as a supported cross-paginator feature, yet the only downstream implementations in this PR either crash on negative offsets (paginator.py:882) or silently clamp them (paginator.py:182), so the sole 'specification' of this untraceable feature is a false statement on a core type.

[ADVISORY] The diff ships a new ~70-line get_result state machine (OptimizedCursorPaginator), the role gate in the endpoint, and a semantics change to shared offset slicing (lines 179-184) with no test anywhere in the diff touching any of them. A regression in the new boundary handling or the shared clamp silently changes 500-vs-clamp and page-boundary behavior for every paginated endpoint in the API with no CI signal, and the off-by-one-prone is_prev arithmetic (`len(results) == offset + limit + extra`) is precisely the behavior whose absence of coverage lets drift between the two get_result copies go undetected.

[BUG] `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally on every request, but `organization_context` is never assigned anywhere in `get()` (the method's locals are queryset/query/event). Every GET to the organization audit log endpoint by a non-superuser raises NameError and returns a 500 — only superusers survive via the `or` short-circuit — so the audit-log API and the Settings UI behind it hard-fail for the entire regular user base, regardless of whether the client ever sends optimized_pagination.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator extends BasePaginator but its get_result is a verbatim copy of Paginator.get_result, calling self.build_queryset (line 857), self._is_asc (line 840), and self.desc (line 903) — members that are defined only on the Paginator subclass and never on BasePaginator. get_result raises AttributeError: 'OptimizedCursorPaginator' object has no attribute 'build_queryset' on the first cursor-keyed queryset build, so the optimized path 500s for every request that reaches it; the class cannot return a single page and should subclass Paginator instead of BasePaginator.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.__init__ forwards **kwargs to BasePaginator.__init__, whose signature (queryset, key, on_results, actor, max_limit) does not accept the desc kwarg that the paginate plumbing derives from order_by='-datetime' (the same translation that configures DateTimePaginator), so the desc=True the endpoint's call produces is rejected at construction. The first superuser request with optimized_pagination=true fails inside paginate() with TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'desc' → 500; the paginator cannot even be instantiated for the endpoint it was written for.

[BUG] get_item_key returns int(math.floor(value)) / int(math.ceil(value)) applied to getattr(item, self.key), and for this endpoint the key is the datetime field (derived from order_by='-datetime'), so math.floor is applied to a datetime object and raises TypeError. Even after the inheritance and constructor defects are fixed, any optimized-path request that returns at least one audit-log row 500s with 'must be a real number, not datetime.datetime' — the paginator cannot key the very queryset it was built to paginate.

[BUG] The negative-offset branch executes list(queryset[start_offset:stop]) with start_offset = cursor.offset < 0, which Django's QuerySet slicing rejects with AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported on querysets.') — the exact opposite of the line-876 comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. The only behavioral capability the class advertises — negative-offset traversal — produces an unhandled exception: an admin client presenting a cursor token carrying a negative offset (cursor payloads are client-controlled) receives a 500 instead of the promised bidirectional pagination, so the feature the PR is named for does not exist.

[ADVISORY] The slicing in the shared get_result (the core paginator family used by this endpoint's default path and many other APIs) is rewritten unconditionally — no flag, and this class has no enable_advanced_features — so a forged cursor with a negative offset now clamps to 0 and silently returns page 1 instead of erroring, while is_prev cursors with negative offsets still hit the ORM's negative-slicing assert. Every endpoint paginating through this class — far beyond audit logs — now accepts corrupt cursor tokens as silently-wrong data windows (clients loop back to page 1 with no error), and the added comment ('efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning') documents a mechanism the clamp does not perform; an audit-log PR changed unrelated endpoints' behavior with no way to turn it off.

[ADVISORY] The new code path is selected by a raw, undocumented query parameter compared with strict string equality (request.GET.get('optimized_pagination') == 'true') and has no feature flag, options entry, or API documentation. Operations cannot disable the crashing admin path without a code deploy (no kill switch), and a client that 'enables' it with any other spelling (1, True, yes) silently falls back to the default path while believing it is optimized; the parameter is an invisible public contract surface absent from the endpoint's options payload.

[ADVISORY] The 'performance' branch is privilege-gated on is_superuser/has_global_access even though both branches execute the identical, already-permission-filtered queryset, creating a parallel admin-only paginator that mints cursor tokens in a different encoding (int(math.floor(...)) keys) than the DateTimePaginator cursors the endpoint otherwise returns — and the paginator comment 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' answers a security objection the branch never had. The org admins and members who actually browse high-volume audit logs — the audience the PR names — never receive the claimed optimization (only superusers do), and a cursor token minted under one mode resolves under the other mode's key scheme (shared links/bookmarks across users with different privileges), silently corrupting pagination; the endpoint now maintains two diverging cursor dialects indefinitely.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result's else-branch duplicates the slicing/boundary logic just modified in the shared get_result (lines 179-184), with the two copies already carrying contradictory justifying comments (one claims the ORM handles negative slicing, the other claims queryset-level permission safety) and divergent gating. The next change to pagination boundary handling must be applied identically in two classes or they silently drift — drift this diff already exhibits between its own comments — where subclassing Paginator and overriding only the slicing would delete the entire copied body (build_queryset call, prev-trim, reverse, build_cursor plumbing).

[ADVISORY] The entire OptimizedCursorPaginator is a copy of the existing Paginator.get_result whose reachable branch issues the same build_queryset filter, the same [offset:stop] slice, and the same count_hits as the default path — the diff contains no query-level optimization for high-volume audit logs anywhere (no index, no keyset-strategy change, no count avoidance). After the crash defects are fixed the class delivers exactly zero performance delta, so reviewers and operators believe a perf problem was solved when nothing changed; deleting the class, the query parameter, and the privilege gate removes ~120 lines from a core module with no functional loss — the correct final shape of this PR is empty.

[ADVISORY] The hunk adds only comments to Cursor.__init__ asserting it now 'allows negative offsets ... enabling efficient reverse pagination' while changing zero behavior — and every Django-backed consumer of Cursor raises on a negative offset, so the comment documents a capability that exists nowhere in the system. The next developer building cursor features reads the constructor of the pagination system's core value object as a supported contract and ships negative-offset cursors that 500 in production — the exact failure this PR's paginator branch already demonstrates at runtime.

[ADVISORY] The artifact silently swaps the accepted objective (pagination performance on audit logs) for a second, unaccepted objective: an undocumented, privilege-gated alternate pagination mode selected by a raw client query parameter ('optimized_pagination=true') with no feature flag, options entry, or API documentation, gated on a brand-new authorization predicate (request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access) that this endpoint never had. Reviewers who accepted a performance tweak have shipped a hidden admin-only API surface on a compliance-sensitive audit-log endpoint that operators cannot disable without a code deploy; the OptimizedCursorPaginator docstring (src/sentry/api/paginator.py:826-831) even sells the change as 'backward compatibility with existing cursor implementations' while introducing negative-offset slicing behavior that no existing paginator performs.

[BUG] The optimized branch passes enable_advanced_features=True to self.paginate(), whose definition in src/sentry/api/base.py declares a fixed parameter list (request, queryset, paginator_cls, on_results, max_limit, desc, cursor, count_hits, known_hits, max_hits, order_by, post_query_filter, sampler, silent_pagination, permit_null_cursor) with no **kwargs, so the call raises TypeError: paginate() got an unexpected keyword argument 'enable_advanced_features'. Every request that takes the new branch returns a 500, so the advertised optimization is unusable as shipped; and even if the kwarg were plumbed through, the module-level paginate() constructs the paginator without forwarding unknown kwargs, leaving enable_advanced_features permanently False — a silent no-op public surface on the new class whose only distinctive behavior (the negative-offset branch) is unreachable by construction.

[BUG] organization_context is not defined anywhere in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get (the method's arguments are request and organization), and the expression request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access is evaluated unconditionally before the use_optimized check, so every request from a non-superuser — where the 'or' fails to short-circuit — raises NameError. The entire audit-log endpoint returns a 500 for all non-superuser callers, including org admins who never pass the new parameter — a full outage of audit-log access hidden inside a PR accepted as a performance optimization.

[BUG] The shared BasePaginator.get_result edit clamps negative offsets only for non-prev cursors (max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset), so a prev cursor carrying a negative client-supplied offset still slices the queryset from a negative index and raises Django's AssertionError 'Negative indexing is not supported', directly contradicting the added comment that 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions'. Every endpoint inheriting this paginator — not just audit logs — now has two contradictory negative-offset behaviors: prev cursors still 500 exactly as before the safety comment, while non-prev cursors silently return the first page where they previously errored — a shared-pagination semantics change accepted on the strength of a false safety claim.

[BUG] With enable_advanced_features set and a cursor whose offset is negative, the advanced branch evaluates list(queryset[start_offset:stop]) with start_offset < 0, which Django rejects on evaluation with AssertionError 'Negative indexing is not supported' — the added comment at line 876 ('The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically') is false. An authorized admin sending ?optimized_pagination=true with a cursor carrying a negative offset (cursor payloads are unsigned, client-controlled base64 JSON) gets a 500 from the audit-log endpoint instead of the 'efficient bidirectional traversal' the comments promise.

[ADVISORY] The new OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result and the endpoint's optimized branch ship with zero tests, and the two ship-breaking defects in this PR — the TypeError on the unsupported paginate kwarg and the AssertionError on negative queryset slicing — are exactly what a single request-level test of GET ?optimized_pagination=true would have caught. Admin audit-log pagination ships broken and stays broken: a regression in the untested negative-offset branch, the prev-trimming arithmetic at line 891, or cursor propagation through build_cursor will never be caught by CI because no test exercises this code path.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates the existing datetime paginator's get_item_key/value_from_cursor verbatim plus ~40 lines of get_result, and re-implements the base paginator's negative-offset policy with a contradictory rule (pass-through-negative at lines 880-882 vs clamp-to-zero at lines 182-184), so one concept now has two hand-maintained, already-divergent implementations in the same file. The next cursor-semantics fix must be applied in three get_result copies; a maintainer fixing the clamp in BasePaginator will reasonably miss the clone, and the already-present divergence is precisely what makes the advanced branch crash — the entire 95-line class plus the endpoint branch is deletable with zero functional loss since DateTimePaginator already provides the accepted pagination semantics.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result feeds a client-forged negative cursor offset straight into queryset slicing, and Django raises "Negative indices are not allowed when slicing QuerySets" for negative slice bounds, so the branch written specifically to enable negative offsets throws an unhandled exception instead of paginating. Any superuser or global-access member requesting /api/0/organizations/<org>/auditlogs/?optimized_pagination=true with a forged cursor (base64 'value:offset:is_prev', e.g. b64('0:-5:1')) receives an HTTP 500; even if Python asserts were stripped, Django clamps the negative low mark to 0, so the promised 'efficient bidirectional pagination' never happens — the feature is either a crash or a silent no-op, and both in-code safety claims ('The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level') are false.

[BUG] The modified paginator get_result clamps negative offsets only in the non-prev case (start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset), so a forged prev cursor carrying a negative offset still reaches queryset[-n:stop] and raises the negative-index error that the new comment claims the queryset 'will handle'. A one-line forged cursor (cursor=b64('0:-5:1')) produces an unhandled 500 on this endpoint's default (non-optimized) pagination path and on every other endpoint using this paginator, for any user with read access — the PR advertises negative-offset support but leaves the primary is_prev path both crashing and mislabeled as safe.

[ADVISORY] The endpoint lets the client select between two paginator implementations sharing the same cursor format via the raw query param optimized_pagination, with no feature flag and with already-divergent boundary semantics between the two paths. An administrator who pages audit logs with the param set on one request and unset on the next (or replays a shared/bookmarked cursor URL under the other setting) gets silently shifted or duplicated windows — skipped audit rows during an incident investigation — and operations has no flag to disable the new path without a code deploy.

[ADVISORY] The diff declares negative offsets a supported Cursor state ('Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios') but adds no validation at the parse/constructor choke point, so self.offset = int(offset) still accepts arbitrary negative ints from the client-forged base64 cursor. Every paginator consumer must now independently guard negative offsets, and the two downstream sites shipped in this same diff already failed to (both crash); the next paginator author who trusts the new comment inherits the same 500 — the enforcement belongs in from_string/__init__ (reject or clamp), not in each caller's slicing logic.

[ADVISORY] The copied prev-trim block in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result drifts from its own slicing: results are sliced using start_offset but the drop condition checks len(results) == offset + limit + extra against the raw cursor offset. Whoever fixes the negative-slice crash by clamping start_offset inherits a silent row-drop here — whenever start_offset != offset (clamped or negative offsets) the elif trims the wrong end and a prev page loses an audit entry with no error, which is precisely the drift that duplicating this ~90-line get_result guarantees.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates the existing DateTimePaginator get_result almost line-for-line while its only behavioral delta (the negative-offset branch) is broken, so the class fails the deletion test: nothing it does works that DateTimePaginator does not already do. Deleting the class, the enable_advanced_features constructor param, the endpoint's optimized_pagination branch, and both negative-offset edits (keeping only the one-line max(0, offset) clamp if negative cursors are meant to be tolerated) removes every line in this PR that can 500 or mis-page; keeping it adds a second pagination implementation to maintain for a feature that cannot exist against a database queryset, since SQL OFFSET cannot be negative.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result's defining feature slices the queryset at a negative cursor.offset (line 880, start_offset = cursor.offset), which Django QuerySet slicing rejects with 'Negative indexing is not supported', so the paginator 500s on exactly the negative-offset cursors it exists to serve, and the line 876 comment claiming the ORM 'properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. An administrator calling GET on the audit-logs endpoint with optimized_pagination=true and any negative-offset cursor receives a 500; the diff contains no test-file changes (its only files are organization_auditlogs.py, paginator.py, and cursors.py), the class is constructed solely by the new endpoint branch gated on a param string that first appears in this diff, and no test written before this diff can reference a class or param introduced by it, so no test anywhere executes this code path and the crash reaches production admins undetected.

[BUG] The rewritten slicing in CursorPaginator.get_result silently clamps negative-offset next-cursors to offset 0 (line 182) while prev-cursors keep slicing at the raw negative offset, so the change delivers neither the bidirectional negative-offset pagination its new comment advertises nor the previous uniform error. Every cursor-paginated endpoint in the API (CursorPaginator is the base of DateTimePaginator and all cursor paginator subclasses) now returns the dataset's first page — rows the client already consumed — for a next-cursor carrying a negative offset where the API previously raised, while the identical crafted cursor on a prev-cursor still 500s; the diff ships no test for the new clamp branch and no pre-existing test can assert semantics introduced by this line, so CI stays green while paging behavior changes API-wide.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/api/paginator.py` the shared `BasePaginator.get_result` was changed to compute `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, and then slice `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. If a client supplies a negative `cursor.offset` with `cursor.is_prev == True`, `start_offset` remains negative and Django queryset slicing with a negative start is not supported (raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`). This directly contradicts the added comment claiming boundary conditions are handled safely, and it introduces inconsistent behavior: non-prev cursors now clamp negatives to 0 while prev cursors can still error. The diff also explicitly preserves/encourages negative offsets (`Cursor.offset = int(offset)` with a comment), making the issue reachable.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] With enable_advanced_features set and a cursor whose offset is negative, the advanced branch evaluates list(queryset[start_offset:stop]) with start_offset < 0, which Django rejects on evaluation with AssertionError 'Negative indexing is not supported' — the added comment at line 876 ('The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically') is false. An authorized admin sending ?optimized_pagination=true with a cursor carrying a negative offset (cursor payloads are unsigned, client-controlled base64 JSON) gets a 500 from the audit-log endpoint instead of the 'efficient bidirectional traversal' the comments promise.

adjudication.rationale: The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` explicitly allows `start_offset = cursor.offset` when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, and then slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. There is no validation/clamping in that branch, and the comments claim negative slicing is handled automatically. Separately, the earlier change to the existing paginator also allows `start_offset = offset` when `cursor.is_prev` (which can also be negative). This introduces a concrete risk of runtime failure when a negative offset is present, rather than providing the advertised behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result and the endpoint's optimized branch ship with zero tests, and the two ship-breaking defects in this PR — the TypeError on the unsupported paginate kwarg and the AssertionError on negative queryset slicing — are exactly what a single request-level test of GET ?optimized_pagination=true would have caught. Admin audit-log pagination ships broken and stays broken: a regression in the untested negative-offset branch, the prev-trimming arithmetic at line 891, or cursor propagation through build_cursor will never be caught by CI because no test exercises this code path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces/expands negative-offset queryset slicing paths that can break at runtime. In `src/sentry/api/paginator.py` the modified `get_result` now does `start_offset = ... if not cursor.is_prev else offset` and then slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]`; if `cursor.is_prev` and `cursor.offset` is negative, this becomes negative slicing. The newly added `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` goes further and explicitly slices with a negative start when `enable_advanced_features` and `cursor.offset < 0` (`results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset = cursor.offset`). Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing/slicing and will raise (commonly an `AssertionError`). The finding’s mention of an unsupported `paginate` kwarg is not verifiable from this diff alone, but the negative-slicing failure mode is grounded in the added code path and would break the optimized/admin branch.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates the existing datetime paginator's get_item_key/value_from_cursor verbatim plus ~40 lines of get_result, and re-implements the base paginator's negative-offset policy with a contradictory rule (pass-through-negative at lines 880-882 vs clamp-to-zero at lines 182-184), so one concept now has two hand-maintained, already-divergent implementations in the same file. The next cursor-semantics fix must be applied in three get_result copies; a maintainer fixing the clamp in BasePaginator will reasonably miss the clone, and the already-present divergence is precisely what makes the advanced branch crash — the entire 95-line class plus the endpoint branch is deletable with zero functional loss since DateTimePaginator already provides the accepted pagination semantics.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly adds a new 95-line `OptimizedCursorPaginator` that re-implements substantial pagination logic already present in `BasePaginator.get_result` (including offset/extra handling, prev-cursor trimming, reverse, `build_cursor`, and `post_query_filter`). It also introduces a second, different negative-offset policy: `BasePaginator.get_result` clamps `start_offset = max(0, offset)` for non-`is_prev` but otherwise uses `offset` directly, while `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` has an additional branch that explicitly passes through negative offsets only when `enable_advanced_features` and `cursor.offset < 0`, otherwise falling back to the (already nontrivial) shared logic. This duplication/divergence is a concrete maintainability/architecture issue created by the change (future cursor/offset fixes must be applied in multiple places), but the finding’s claims about a definite crash and that it’s deletable “with zero functional loss” are not verifiable from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result feeds a client-forged negative cursor offset straight into queryset slicing, and Django raises "Negative indices are not allowed when slicing QuerySets" for negative slice bounds, so the branch written specifically to enable negative offsets throws an unhandled exception instead of paginating. Any superuser or global-access member requesting /api/0/organizations/<org>/auditlogs/?optimized_pagination=true with a forged cursor (base64 'value:offset:is_prev', e.g. b64('0:-5:1')) receives an HTTP 500; even if Python asserts were stripped, Django clamps the negative low mark to 0, so the promised 'efficient bidirectional pagination' never happens — the feature is either a crash or a silent no-op, and both in-code safety claims ('The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level') are false.

Django QuerySet slicing does not permit negative indices and will raise an exception (commonly an `AssertionError` about negative indexing), which would surface as a 500 if not caught. The diff also shows `Cursor.offset` is accepted as any int (no validation), and the endpoint explicitly enables this paginator/feature for privileged users (`enable_advanced_features=True`), making the crash reachable via a forged cursor.

A one-line forged cursor (cursor=b64('0:-5:1')) produces an unhandled 500 on this endpoint's default (non-optimized) pagination path and on every other endpoint using this paginator, for any user with read access — the PR advertises negative-offset support but leaves the primary is_prev path both crashing and mislabeled as safe.

Since `Cursor.offset` is directly `int(offset)` from the cursor payload (no clamping in `sentry/utils/cursors.py`), a crafted prev-cursor with a negative `offset` will pass a negative start index into Django queryset slicing, which Django rejects (`AssertionError: Negative indexes are not allowed in queryset slicing`). adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/api/paginator.py` the slicing logic changed from `queryset[offset:stop]` to `queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset = max(0, offset)` for non-`prev` cursors. This is a behavior change that can cause silent duplication/missing entries for consumers with buggy cursor arithmetic, and it affects any endpoint using this paginator method (not just the audit log endpoint).
